The 5-GW dc dc annual cell tariff rate quota was almost reached in 2023 and was passed for 2024 within the first half of the year. To avoid increased costs to U.S. module assembly operations, the tariff rate quota was extended to 12.5 GW . That higher mark was reached on December 30, 2024. The dc annually reset 12.5-GW limit for duty-free cell imports was reached in July 2025. Once the cell dc tariff rate quota is met, the Section 201 duties are 14%, on top of any other duties or tariffs. For example, the AD/CVD on imported cells is 8.6% for most cells shipped from Malaysia and 125% for shipments from Cambodia (U.S. International Trade Administration 2025b). Only a trace of imports from Cambodia can be found within the U.S. trade data in Q3 2024. Cell imports from Malaysia and other countries in ASEAN, including Indonesia and Laos, increased substantially in 2024. Section 201 duties are set to expire on February 7, 2026. A U.S. cell counts significantly toward the domestic content bonus credit, and this could deter exports in the future as well. 2.4.4 Regional Costs for Crystalline-Silicon Cells Figure 16 shows NLR-calculated PERC cell costs by region. Outside China, variations in equipment and facilities CapEx as well as materials costs are driven by distance from suppliers, trade policies, manufacturing experience, and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) costs. The materials and equipment for cell manufacturing can be entirely Chinese supplied, although some materials are available from ASEAN and some manufacturing equipment from the European Union. China’s supply chain advantages drive their cost advantage. All countries outside China are relatively inexperienced, which also impacts EPC costs, and the United States and Europe have higher labor and management costs for EPC. The contributors to direct cost of goods sold vary by location. In the United States, Section 301 tariffs on some materials supplied from China can add 25% (see Section 2.4.5).
